newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Renegade Tajik commander's tanks leave Tursunzade.
newsitem.headline: Renegade Tajik commander's tanks leave Tursunzade.

text.p: A renegade Tajik commander has removed tanks and troops from a disputed aluminium-producing town but it is unclear whether he has patched up differences with the president of the former Soviet republic.
The street by administration building in the western Tajikistan town of Tursunzade's, which had been chock full of armour and troops on Thursday, was virtually empty on Friday.

Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, who led an armed rebellion against the shaky government of President Imomali Rakhmonov last year, sent his elite armoured brigade into Tursunzade on Wednesday to unseat local strongman Kodir Abdulayev.
The town, 45 km (30 miles) west of the capital Dushanbe, is home to a large aluminium smelter over which armed gangs have fought for control in recent months.
Rakhmonov ordered the commander back to barracks. "His actions were illegal," said presidential spokesman Zafar Saidov. "We hope he obeys orders and returns back to barracks."
But while the tanks had left the centre of the town, it was far from clear where they were headed.
The town's newly-installed administration said Khudoyberdyev had left for his base in Kurgan-Tyube in the south.
But rumours in the town said the commander had merely hidden his tanks inside the sprawling aluminium plant, though only one light armoured vehicle was visible, posted on the factory gates.
Russia's Itar-Tass news agency said the brigade had clashed once more with Abdulayev's forces near the border with Uzbekistan early on Friday.
The Tajik capital Dushanbe itself was calm and armoured vehicles guarded the roads leading into the town.
However, diplomats say the disobedient commander underlined Rakhmonov's weak hold on the mountainous country of 5.7 million.

"Colonels disobey his orders, negotiators ignore his commands and regional officials ignore his directives," said a Western diplomat in Dushanbe who asked not to be named. "He's the weakest kind of executive there is."
Diplomats estimate Rakhmonov probably controls only 15-20 percent of the country, while the Islamist guerrillas hold nearly half.
The diplomat said Khudoyberdyev was politically ambitious and bitter at talks between the government and the Islamist opposition which has fought a bloody four-year civil war.
"The timing is perfect, the two sides are only three days into the talks," the diplomat said, referring to peace negotiations underway in the Iranian capital Tehran.
The talks are aimed at hammering out a power-sharing deal, doling out 40 percent of government positions to each side.
The remaining 20 percent would to go to the northern Tajik faction based in Khudzhand (Leninabad).
A ceasefire confirmed in Moscow last month seems to be holding.
But many factions in the republic, now prey to a kaleidescopic array of armed bands pushing regional, clan and economic interests, are worried they could be sidelined in the talks.
Khudoyberdyev himself told reporters on Thursday: "I'm not interested in the (peace) accord, I don't believe in it."

Observers say Rakhmonov's continued hold on power is guaranteed only by Russia's troop presence in Tajikistan, where its soldiers carry out peacekeeping duties and guard the republic's frontiers with Afghanistan and China.
